4.4. Implications for digital heritage

In addition to improving accuracy and F1, the integrated pipeline 
has broader implications for digital heritage applications. First, the Top-
3 accuracies above 0.5 across pamor, dhapur, and tangguh indicate that 
the system can function effectively as a decision-support tool. Even 
when top-1 predictions are uncertain, ranked outputs provide curators 
with plausible candidate sets for triage, cataloguing, and provenance 
assessment. This is especially valuable in heritage contexts, where 
expert resources are limited and inter-expert agreement is not always 
guaranteed (Foka & Griffin, 2024). Importantly, we position the pro-
posed model as assistive rather than substitutive: it is intended to 
support expert workflows by narrowing plausible categories, while final 
interpretation and attribution remain with human experts.

Second, the reproducible preprocessing–augmentation–architecture 
workflow addresses reproducibility and fairness objectives, as empha-
sized in the Introduction. By enforcing standardized backgrounds, con-
sistent orientation, balanced class distributions, and architecture tai-
lored to the elongated blade geometry, the pipeline reduces noise and 
bias in model training. This structured approach offers a transferable 
template for other domains in which subtle textures and complex 
morphologies must be recognized under data scarcity, such as textiles, 
ceramics, and biomedical imaging. In this context, ethical and cultural 
governance is inseparable from technical reproducibility: keris images 
are culturally significant materials that remain under custodial author-
ity, and any reuse or sharing must follow permission-based agreements 
consistent with curatorial and heritage protocols.

Third, the compact 512 × 512 design and lightweight classifier 
head make the system suitable for deployment on mobile and edge 
devices in the future. This design choice aligns with the focus of the 
resume pipeline on deployment readiness and resource efficiency. Com-
parable initiatives in intelligent systems suggest that such portability 
can democratize access to AI, enabling community-level engagement 
with cultural heritage while reducing dependence on centralized, high-
performance infrastructure (Merizzi et al., 2024; Wang & Zhu, 2022). 
Together, these implications extend the contribution of KerisRDNet 
beyond academic benchmarks toward practical integration for digital 
heritage preservation and dissemination. Where expert disagreements 
are unavoidable in fine-grained attribution, our data curation process 
reflects this reality by reconciling labels through expert discussion 
and verification and excluding unresolved cases, thereby avoiding the 
propagation of uncertain ground truth into downstream models.
4.5. Generalizability and challenges

Although the proposed pipeline achieved consistent improvements 
across both fine- and coarse-grained tasks, several challenges remain. 
Confusion persisted in visually adjacent classes, reflecting the intrinsic 
difficulty of discriminating subtle morphological or textural differences, 
even for experts. Although the dataset was carefully curated and aug-
mented, it remained modest in size, which limited the model’s exposure 
to the full diversity of keris artifacts. Robustness to domain shifts, such 
as variations in lighting, imaging hardware, or surface degradation, 
was not directly evaluated. Preprocessing and augmentation reduce but 
cannot fully eliminate these risks, indicating that broader digitization 
campaigns and cross-institutional validation are required to ensure 
wide applicability.

Despite these constraints, this study positions keris recognition 
as a proxy for fine-grained classification in low-data, high-variability 
regimes. This perspective highlights that the challenges observed here 
are not unique to cultural heritage but resonate with other intelligent 
system applications under similar conditions. Therefore, future work 
should pursue multi-task learning that jointly models pamor, dhapur, 
and tangguh, explore interpretable attention mechanisms to enhance 
transparency for curators, and investigate self-supervised or transfer 
learning to strengthen generalization under data scarcity. Federated

and cross-institutional approaches may also enable scaling while re-
specting custodial restrictions. These directions point toward more 
robust, interpretable, and ethically responsible intelligent systems for 
cultural heritage and related fields.

To support reproducibility, we provide a public repository contain-
ing the implementation and configuration files for the preprocessing, 
augmentation, training, and evaluation pipeline, including runnable 
scripts that export the main quantitative results (e.g., CSV metrics 
summaries and confusion matrices) for table reproduction. Due to cul-
tural custodianship and governance constraints, the full dataset cannot 
be publicly released; the repository therefore documents the required 
local data layout and provides an optional small anonymized sample 
subset where permitted by the custodians. Where allowed, trained 
weights are also provided via the repository. Third-party tools and 
their licenses/terms (including rembg and YOLOv8/ultralytics) 
are listed in a dedicated third-party notices file in the repository. 
Repository: https://github.com/masaboe/Keris-RDIN.
5. Limitations and future work

This study also highlights several areas for improvement that frame 
directions for future research. Although mask-aware augmentation in-
creased the dataset balance, the underlying corpus remained modest 
and could not capture the full diversity of keris artifacts or the range 
of degradations found in real-world collections. Residual ambiguities in 
visually adjacent classes, particularly among sibling pamor motifs and 
morphologically similar dhapur motifs, continue to pose challenges. 
In addition, the decision process of KerisRDNet remains difficult to 
interpret for non-technical users, and dataset sharing is constrained 
by cultural custodianship, which limits the opportunities for external 
benchmarking.

In addition, robustness under explicit curator- or acquisition-setting 
domain shifts was not evaluated in this study through held-out
acquisition-source splits or controlled perturbation experiments (e.g.,
lighting or sensor changes). Curator-held-out evaluation and calibration 
assessment under such shifts (e.g., ECE/Brier) are therefore identified 
as important directions for future cross-institutional validation when 
acquisition-source annotations become available.
Future work can address these challenges in three main directions.

• Methodological: Multi-task learning frameworks that jointly
model pamor, dhapur, and tangguh could leverage shared features 
across categories, while interpretable attention-based visualiza-
tion would improve transparency for curators.
• Architectural: Benchmarking KerisRDNet against transformer-
based models such as ViT or Swin may reveal complementary 
strengths in capturing long-range dependencies and subtle surface 
patterns.
• Scalability and sustainability: Efficiency analyses are needed to 
assess trade-offs between accuracy and computational cost, and 
federated or cross-institutional learning strategies offer a path-
way to scaling without compromising data ownership or cultural 
sensitivities.
6. Conclusion

This study presents a domain-specific deep learning pipeline for 
keris classification as a case of fine-grained cultural heritage recogni-
tion. The pipeline combined standardized preprocessing, mask-aware 
augmentation, and the proposed KerisRDNet architecture tailored with 
IRD blocks and a squeeze-and-excitation mechanism. Together, these 
components stabilized the inputs, mitigated the imbalance, and im-
proved the discriminative capacity where the generic backbones failed.

Across pamor (27 classes), dhapur (42 classes), and tangguh (5 
classes), the pipeline achieved directionally consistent gains across 
resamplings, supported by paired analyses, interpreted conservatively

given 𝑛= 3, raising the macro-F1 well above near-zero baselines and 
delivering Top-3 accuracies above 0.5. These outcomes demonstrate 
the practical value of the proposed model as a decision-support tool 
for curators, reducing reliance on manual expertise while preserving 
human oversight.

Beyond keris, the workflow offers a transferable strategy for low-
data fine-grained recognition tasks, balancing accuracy, reproducibil-
ity, and deployment efficiency under the evaluated experimental set-
ting. By aligning domain-specific engineering with rigorous evaluation, 
KerisRDNet contributes both a functional tool for cultural preservation 
and a generalizable approach for fine-grained classification under data 
scarcity.
